questions.instructions: Who published the text, and in what role?

options.description: A company reporting its own news.
A law firm or agent seeking clients or claimants about another company.
An analyst, a research seller or a media outlet writing about another company.
A regulator, a central bank, a court or an exchange.
None of these: no company's event is reported.

questions.instructions: What kind of content does the text carry? A product, research or technology release is a new event, however ordinary it is for the company that makes it.

options.description: It reports a specific new event or decision.
It is a scheduled or administrative notice with no new event.
It promotes a company, a product or a view without a new event.
It is not about a company's event.

questions.instructions: Does the text state a specific development with a date, an amount or a named counterparty attached?

options.description: It names a dated action, an amount or a counterparty.
It is commentary, promotion or a general statement.

questions.instructions: Whom does the reported event concern?

options.description: Only the company the text is mainly about.
That company and other companies the text names.
A whole category of companies, such as an industry or the users of a technology.

questions.instructions: Does the text describe a category of companies, other than its subject, that the event bears on?

options.description: The reported event improves its business, finances or standing.
The reported event harms its business, finances or standing.
The text does not say enough to tell.

questions.instructions: How much does the reported event change the business, finances or standing of the text's main company? Judge that company alone, not other companies.

options.description: No change: a routine, administrative or promotional notice.
A small or ordinary change, one of many in its normal course.
A large change to its results, leadership, financing or legal position.
Its control, its survival or the core of its business is at stake.

questions.instructions: Is a state body involved in the reported event: a government, a regulator, a prosecutor, an intelligence service or a court?
Does the text state criminal or national-security allegations?
Is the reported departure or action forced or made under pressure, not voluntary?

options.description: It is forced or under pressure.
It is voluntary, or the text does not say.

questions.instructions: Does the matter reach beyond one country: several governments, jurisdictions or national markets?
Does the text state how large the reported event is: an amount, a percentage, a count or a share?
If the text states how large the reported event is, how large is it against what it changes: the revenue, outlook, workforce, shares, assets or debt it is a part of?

options.description: No size is stated, or nothing to compare it with.
Under about a tenth of what it changes, or the text calls it not material.
About a tenth or more of what it changes, or the text calls it substantial or material.

questions.instructions: Does the text say the reported event was announced earlier, planned or expected?

It names a permanent one, or none, or no person changes.

How does the reported event bear on a category of companies other than its subject?

options.description: It shows that what those companies sell or build works or is wanted.
It makes it cheaper or easier for those companies to operate.
It opens a market or a customer group to those companies.
The subject starts to do itself what those companies sell.
The subject offers something that replaces what those companies sell.
It states or shows that what those companies sell is far from useful or wanted.
It bears on such a category in none of these ways.
The text names no such category, or does not say enough.

questions.instructions: Does the text report something that lowers costs or barriers for companies other than its subject?
Does the text report the subject entering a market other companies already serve?
Does the text report the subject adopting, buying or endorsing a technology other companies supply?
Does the text report something offered as a replacement for what other companies sell?
Does the text state that a technology or product category is not ready, not useful or not wanted?

How much does the reported event matter to a category of companies other than the text's main company? Judge those companies alone: an event that is ordinary for the main company can matter greatly to them.

options.description: The text describes no such category, or the event does not bear on one.
It bears on such a category in a small or incidental way.
It changes what those companies can build, sell or charge, or what they compete with.
It removes or creates a main obstacle to what those companies do.

questions.instructions: Does the reported event matter more to other companies than to the text's main company?

options.description: It does not, or it concerns no other companies.

questions.instructions: Does the text show its main company as large or leading, and the other companies the event bears on as smaller or specialised in one field?
Does the text's main company give away, open or standardise something other companies need: open models, tools, interfaces or reference designs?
Does the text name a category of other companies, or a problem they face, as the purpose of what is released or done?
Where does the cause of the reported event lie?

options.description: In the subject company alone: its management, its accounts, its product, its contract.
In a condition shared by its industry: demand, prices, regulation, a supplier, a technology.
